rationale: The official PMC HTML contains 808 individually headed member articles. The member on excessive nutmeg use reports auditory hallucinations, mania and insomnia. A separate dementia-with-Lewy-bodies case describes visual hallucinations. An electroconvulsive-therapy review summarizes earlier DLB case reports. The inspected members do not pair dried fig ingestion with visual hallucination frequency.

The official PMC HTML contains 206 numbered member headings. The EASE LID 2 subgroup, CVT-301 drug safety analysis and pimavanserin chart review report different medication exposures and measures. Separate SCA17 and MPAN cases describe complex or visual hallucinations. The PKAN report names a disorder and gene pathway, without a dietary B5 arm or dried fig comparison.

The authors summarize subregional insular atrophy across neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. Symptoms are discussed as clinical correlates of imaging. The review supplies no separately measured visual episode response after dried fig ingestion.

The investigators compared 154 familial and 137 sporadic dementia-with-Lewy-bodies patients. CSF Alzheimer biomarker status differed between groups, and the study assessed first symptoms, cognitive trajectories and family history. Visual hallucination is part of the clinical diagnosis; there is no food-specific contrast.

The review discusses neuroimaging for eye disorders, optic nerve and visual pathway symptoms. It distinguishes complex hallucinations with visual impairment from radiographic findings. The sources provide a differential diagnosis and no dried fig comparison.

This review contrasts anatomic and molecular imaging across dementias. The Lewy body pattern includes visual hallucinations as one clinical feature. The discussion does not compare food intake against symptom occurrence or frequency.

The article reviews cell replacement, tissue engineering and related approaches for Parkinson disease. The treatments and outcomes concern grafts, biological platforms and neuronal function. Hallucination discussion is clinical background, without culinary fig intake.

Nineteen patients with predominantly akinetic-rigid Parkinson disease and twelve controls were recruited. Resting electrophysiological networks were compared with regard to dopamine therapy and diagnosis. The contrast concerns drug effects and physiological networks, without food exposure or visual episode counting.

This study characterizes cognitive and behavioral features across multiple system atrophy subtypes and evaluates the relationship to orthostatic hypotension. The examination and diagnosis differ from a food-timed Parkinson visual hallucination study.

The cohort included 73 people with MCI and Lewy body features and 124 with MCI associated with Alzheimer disease. Visual hallucinations were recorded in 37 of 73 in the Lewy body group, and symptom presence also informed group definition. The follow-up modeled time to dementia, not an incidence rate after dried fig ingestion.

The analysis compares 21 participants with dementia with Lewy bodies, 16 with Parkinson cognitive impairment, and 24 cognitively normal Parkinson participants. MRI cortical thickness and amyloid PET are the measured contrasts. Clinical visual features are not timed against food ingestion.

Cardiac tissue and Lewy body co-pathology were compared in dementia groups including Alzheimer disease. The outcome is cardiac sympathetic innervation. No dried fig intake or clinical visual episode count is measured.

This study uses cortical morphometry in a Huntington disease project with comparison participants. It addresses cortical development and degeneration. The measured imaging variables and population differ from the frozen symptom and no dried fig exposure is present.

The retrospective study evaluates three dopamine transporter SPECT quantification approaches against neuropathology in neurodegenerative syndromes. Hallucination information is clinical characterization. The compared test methods cannot estimate a food effect.

Designer drugs are examined by mechanism and adverse effects, including perceptual changes and hallucinations in some intoxication reports. These are chemically distinct pharmacologic exposures and do not identify the frozen food or Parkinson endpoint comparison.

The review describes VPS35-associated Parkinson disease and experimental retromer mechanisms. Clinical features of genetic carriers and trafficking observations are separate from dietary fig intake or counted hallucinations.

The study compares clinical investigation delays, diagnostic features and treatments of Lewy body and other dementias, and also considers Parkinson dementia. It distinguishes visual and nonvisual symptoms in clinical records. Those records provide no repeated visual event estimate after a culinary exposure.

The study compares alpha-synuclein oligomers and neurofilament light in CSF among multiple system atrophy, Lewy body synucleinopathy and control groups. Biomarker discrimination is the outcome. No fig ingestion and no exposure-linked visual hallucination count were measured.

The article considers motor and nonmotor care, treatment adjustments and complications in late-stage Parkinson disease. Hallucinations are discussed in relation to disease and treatment. There is no original estimate for a fig exposure.

The cohort comprises 19 people with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder, 38 with Parkinson disease and 19 controls. Relative metabolic imaging differences and inferred disease trajectories are the endpoints, distinct from visual hallucination frequency following ingestion.

Dementia brain donors were screened for LRP10 variants and characterized by Lewy and other neuropathology. Clinical visual phenomena are part of phenotype reporting, with no separately varied dried fig exposure.

The study related amyloid and tau markers to atrophy in 86 probable cases. The visual rating scales record radiologic atrophy, and visual hallucinations are clinical context. Neither variable measures an ingestion-linked visual episode response.

The authors review care across ophthalmology and other clinical specialties. They discuss visual problems and hallucinations in the disease and in treatment-related contexts. No dried fig feeding or separately measured hallucination frequency is reported.

The review distinguishes ocular deficits, diplopia, perceptual changes and hallucinations. It discusses visual symptoms and relevant management measures, without an original cohort comparing visual episode rates after dried fruit or figs.

The review collects CNS manifestations in selected inherited muscle diseases. Neuropsychiatric findings are relevant for differential diagnosis. It does not test exposure or visual episode frequency in a Parkinson clinical sample.

This study tests clinical conditions suggestive of progressive supranuclear palsy against autopsy-confirmed diagnoses. Visual hallucination documentation contributes to differential-phenotype discussion, with no dietary intervention or follow-up by food.

The review discusses neuroinflammatory mechanisms and neurological syndromes. Reported manifestations and pathogenic pathways are distinct from culinary fig exposure and quantified Parkinson visual hallucinations.

Sixteen healthy people were recruited. Accelerated but not single-session stimulation reduced GABA+ for up to a day, and basic tested vision and cognition changed little. The reference to hallucinations in other studies concerns damaged visual pathways. This study supplies neither Parkinson clinical symptoms nor a food contrast.

The article discusses whether declining clinical benefit after stimulation reflects habituation or disease progression. The proposed comparisons are clinical and device related. No dried fig exposure or specific visual episode frequency is evaluated.

The review compares trial designs and challenges for dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson dementia. Hallucinations are considered in symptoms and existing drug study outcomes. No food-specific clinical estimate can be extracted.

Clinical records and polysomnography where available were used to classify REM sleep behavior disorder in diagnosed synucleinopathies. The endpoints are timing of dream enactment and diagnosed disease, distinct from waking visual episodes after ingestion.

The work reports expert judgments on behavioral and psychological symptoms and antipsychotic treatment. Visual hallucination is a clinical factor in treatment selection. The consensus gives no observed food-associated symptom change.

The article distinguishes neuropsychiatric symptoms, cognition and the clinical course of Parkinson disease. Hallucination reports are drawn from cited studies and drug management literature, with no original comparison by dried fig ingestion.

Investigators tested an immunohistochemical assay for pathologic alpha-synuclein in skin across sleep behavior disorder, Parkinson disease, atypical parkinsonism and controls. Biopsy assay performance is the outcome; it does not measure exposure-linked visual symptoms.

The report compares 26 people with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder, 137 controls and 223 Parkinson samples, with subgroup differences in available data. Table 2 covers 17 named food and beverage frequencies, including coffee and tea, and does not list fruit or figs. Fecal bacterial profiles are analyzed. The Parkinson visual hallucination reference is background rather than a measured dietary outcome.

Two alpha-synuclein mouse lines were examined for early hippocampal network excitability. The outcome is a laboratory physiological phenotype, without measured dried fig intake or clinical visual hallucinations.

This cohort combines resting-state functional imaging with repeated neuropsychological assessment to evaluate executive decline. Connectivity and cognitive task scores do not count visual episodes after an ingredient exposure.

The report describes visual hallucinations in the course of childhood-onset dystonia, myelopathy and a neurodegenerative syndrome distinct from idiopathic Parkinson disease. It gives no dried fig ingestion comparison or exposure-timed event frequency.

The imaging sample comprises 10 people with dementia with Lewy bodies, 14 healthy controls and 27 in the Alzheimer group. The cited pathology literature discusses visual hallucination occurrence. The study measures tracer patterns and cognition, without an ingestion-linked visual outcome.
